qs.stem: A pharmacist calls: a new prescription reads “methotrexate 15 mg by mouth daily” for RA. What is the safety problem?

options.A: It should be IV only in RA
options.B: It needs N-acetylcysteine with each dose
options.C: It should be weekly; daily dosing can be fatal
options.D: It should be twice daily for steady levels
options.E: Nothing — daily dosing is standard for RA

qs.why: Methotrexate is dosed weekly, not daily — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.

whys.A: The dosing error is frequency, not route.
whys.E: Daily dosing is the dangerous error.

qs.discriminator: The one RA drug where frequency errors kill.

qs.stem: A patient with RA cannot tolerate methotrexate. Which conventional DMARD does the lecture name as the alternative?
qs.why: Leflunomide is the alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.

whys.B: A biologic, not a conventional DMARD.
whys.C: Named as often used in combinations.

qs.takeaway: Methotrexate anchor · HCQ milder · sulfasalazine combos · leflunomide if MTX not tolerated.
qs.discriminator: Conventional (small molecule) vs. biologic DMARDs.

qs.stem: A patient with RA on weekly methotrexate is started on probenecid for gout. Which effect should the clinician anticipate?

options.B: Lower methotrexate levels and RA flares
options.D: Lower penicillin levels if she needs one

qs.why: Probenecid (URAT1 inhibitor) raises levels of penicillins, methotrexate and NSAIDs; it also causes kidney stones (hydrate, alkalinize urine) and is avoided with eGFR under 30 or during a flare.
qs.discriminator: Penicillin adjunct = the same mechanism that raises methotrexate.

qs.stem: Three weeks after starting methotrexate for RA, a patient wants to stop it because the joints still ache. What is the best response?

options.A: Switch to daily dosing to speed the response
options.B: Continue: DMARD protection builds over weeks to months
options.C: Stop it — a DMARD that works relieves pain within days
options.D: Replace it with an NSAID to change the disease course
options.E: Add acetaminophen instead, since RA is degenerative

qs.why: NSAIDs relieve symptoms in days, while DMARDs protect joints over weeks to months; DMARDs modify the disease course rather than just masking symptoms.

whys.A: Methotrexate is weekly only; daily dosing has been fatal.
whys.C: Fast relief in days is the NSAID pattern, not the DMARD one.
whys.D: NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not modify RA.
whys.E: RA is autoimmune; OA is degenerative.

qs.takeaway: DMARDs are slow but change the disease; bridge symptoms, don’t abandon the DMARD.
qs.discriminator: NSAID = fast symptom relief; DMARD = slow disease modification.

qs.stem: A 29-year-old with active RA who is planning a pregnancy needs a DMARD. Which drug from the lecture is contraindicated?

options.A: Celecoxib, because it is a disease-modifying drug
options.B: Sulfasalazine, because it is only used alone
options.C: Acetaminophen, because it is a DMARD
options.E: Hydroxychloroquine, because of its poor safety profile

qs.why: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic (S49).

whys.A: Celecoxib is an NSAID, not a DMARD (S29; S45).
whys.B: Sulfasalazine is often used in combination regimens (S47).
whys.C: Acetaminophen is an analgesic, not a DMARD (S15; S45).
whys.D: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic (S49).
whys.E: Hydroxychloroquine has a relatively favorable safety profile (S47).

qs.stem: A 50-kg woman with mild RA takes hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and has a borderline-long QT on citalopram. Which change best follows the drug profile?

options.A: Stop eye exams since the dose is standard
options.B: Lower the dose to stay within 5 mg/kg/day
options.C: Raise to 600 mg for better RA control
options.D: Keep 400 mg; the maximum is per ideal weight
options.E: Add azithromycin to cover infection risk

qs.why: Hydroxychloroquine: 200–400 mg daily, maximum 5 mg/kg/day actual body weight (here 250 mg). Retinal toxicity needs baseline and annual eye exams; caution with QT-prolonging drugs.

whys.A: Baseline and annual eye exams are needed.
whys.C: Exceeds the maximum and adds QT risk.
whys.D: The limit uses actual body weight: 400 mg = 8 mg/kg.

qs.takeaway: HCQ max 5 mg/kg/day (actual weight); eye exams; QT caution.
qs.discriminator: Do the arithmetic: 400 mg ÷ 50 kg = 8 mg/kg.

qs.stem: Which conventional DMARD requires a baseline eye exam and annual screening after 5 years because of retinopathy?
qs.why: Antimalarials bind melanin-rich tissue such as the retina; a baseline exam and annual screening after 5 years are recommended (p. 684).

whys.A: Methotrexate monitoring targets liver, marrow, and lung (S49).
whys.B: Mycophenolate’s issues are GI, liver, cytopenias, and infection (p. 689).
whys.C: Sulfasalazine’s issues are GI, rash, and cytopenias (p. 690).
whys.D: Leflunomide’s issues are diarrhea and liver tests (p. 688).
whys.E: Antimalarials bind melanin-rich tissue such as the retina; a baseline exam and annual screening after 5 years are recommended (p. 684).

qs.stem: A patient starting sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis has G6PD deficiency and a sulfa allergy. What is the best decision?

options.A: Use sulfasalazine with folic acid 1 mg daily
options.C: Use sulfasalazine and check a CBC monthly
options.D: Skip 5-ASA therapy and start a biologic
options.E: Use sulfasalazine at half the usual dose

qs.why: Sulfasalazine is contraindicated with sulfa or salicylate allergy and causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency (plus agranulocytosis, SJS, folate deficiency). Mesalamine delivers 5-ASA without the sulfa component.

whys.A: Folic acid prevents folate deficiency, not allergy or hemolysis.
whys.C: Sulfa allergy is a contraindication; G6PD raises hemolysis risk.
whys.D: Mild disease starts with 5-ASA — mesalamine fits.
whys.E: Dose reduction does not remove the contraindication.

qs.takeaway: Sulfa allergy or G6PD → avoid sulfasalazine; mesalamine is the 5-ASA alternative.
qs.discriminator: Same active moiety (5-ASA), different carrier — the carrier carries the sulfa risk.

qs.stem: A 29-year-old man with RA on sulfasalazine says his urine is orange and he and his partner have not conceived. Which interpretation is right?

options.B: Infertility is permanent; stop all DMARDs
options.C: Orange urine signals hepatotoxicity, so stop it today
options.D: Expected sulfasalazine effects; sperm count recovers

qs.why: Sulfasalazine adverse effects include orange urine and reversible oligospermia, plus nausea, rash, myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity (monitor CBC and liver tests).

whys.C: Orange urine is a harmless known effect.
whys.E: G6PD raises hemolysis risk; not these findings.

qs.discriminator: Benign-but-alarming effects are common exam bait.

name: Adalimumab
cls: Biologic DMARD · TNF inhibitor (fully human antibody)

Don’t combine biologics (abatacept with a TNF inhibitor raises serious infections).

qs.stem: A 46-year-old with RA not controlled on methotrexate has multiple sclerosis and NYHA class III heart failure. Which biologic choice is least appropriate?
qs.why: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab) are contraindicated with demyelinating disease and NYHA III–IV heart failure, besides active infection and untreated latent TB.

whys.A: Infection, lipids and liver; no demyelination contraindication.
whys.B: No demyelination or heart-failure contraindication listed (caution in COPD).
whys.C: Severe heart failure is listed — but not demyelinating disease.
whys.E: Not ideal, but not harmful in the same way.

qs.takeaway: TNF inhibitor no-gos: demyelinating disease, NYHA III–IV HF, untreated TB.
qs.discriminator: The patient's two comorbidities both point at the same class.

qs.stem: A patient with RA on adalimumab has a family history of lymphoma and asks about cancer risk. Which statement matches the textbook?

options.A: Boxed warnings apply only to IV biologics
options.B: Only methotrexate carries a malignancy warning
options.C: TNF inhibitors carry a boxed malignancy warning
options.D: Cancer risk applies only to JAK inhibitors
options.E: TNF inhibitors lower lymphoma risk to zero

qs.why: The FDA placed a boxed warning on all anti-TNF agents about possible malignancy, especially lymphoma; periodic skin exams are advised.

whys.A: The warning covers all anti-TNF agents.
whys.B: The boxed malignancy warning is on all anti-TNF agents.
whys.D: JAK inhibitors share a cancer warning, but TNF inhibitors have one too.
whys.E: The FDA boxed warning concerns malignancy, especially lymphoma.

qs.takeaway: TNF inhibitors: infection (TB, hepatitis B) + boxed malignancy warning.
qs.discriminator: TNF boxed = malignancy; JAK boxed = VTE, MACE, cancer.

qs.stem: Before starting adalimumab, a patient’s interferon-gamma release assay is positive. What is the most appropriate decision?

options.A: Give a live vaccine first to boost immunity
options.B: Treat latent TB before starting the TNF inhibitor
options.E: Start adalimumab now; TB screening is a formality

qs.why: All DMARDs share infection risk; screen for TB and hepatitis B/C and update vaccines before starting a biologic, treating positives first.

whys.A: Live vaccines are avoided around immunosuppression.
whys.C: Methotrexate is weekly; and TB still needs treatment.

qs.takeaway: Screen → treat → then start the biologic.
qs.discriminator: Biologic risk = infection; fever on a biologic = infection until proven otherwise.

qs.stem: A patient from a region with high tuberculosis rates is about to start adalimumab. Which step matters most before the first dose?

options.D: Screen for TB and hepatitis B/C

qs.discriminator: Shared DMARD risk = infection.

qs.stem: An 84-year-old with a creatinine clearance of 28 mL/min takes famotidine 40 mg twice daily. Over a week she becomes confused and agitated. Infection workup is negative. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

qs.why: Famotidine is renally cleared: reduce the dose when CrCl is below 60 mL/min. Accumulation in CKD causes CNS effects, especially in older adults — a Unit 1 renal-dosing principle applied to a Unit 3 drug.

qs.takeaway: H2 blockers: reduce dose when CrCl < 60; confusion in older adults with CKD.
qs.discriminator: Accumulation (renal) vs. interaction (CYP) — famotidine is the renal one.

qs.stem: A patient on spironolactone for hyperaldosteronism also takes lisinopril. What should be monitored?
qs.why: Spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor; ACEi/ARBs and potassium add to hyperkalemia.
qs.discriminator: Gynecomastia is the other classic effect.

qs.stem: A patient taking lisinopril and furosemide develops an acute gout flare. Which plan avoids the most predictable kidney injury?

options.A: Probenecid to flush uric acid through the kidney
options.B: Start allopurinol today to shorten the flare
options.D: Avoid an NSAID; treat with a short corticosteroid course
options.E: Celecoxib, because COX-2 selectivity spares the kidney

qs.why: NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic is the high-yield ‘triple whammy’ AKI pattern; a short corticosteroid course is a good flare alternative when NSAIDs are contraindicated.

whys.A: Chronic ULT, also avoided in renal impairment.
whys.B: ULT is deferred until the flare resolves.
whys.C: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is the ‘triple whammy’ for AKI.

qs.takeaway: Check the medication list before choosing a flare drug.
qs.discriminator: Celecoxib protects the stomach, not the kidney.

qs.stem: A stage 3 CKD patient on lisinopril starts spironolactone; two weeks later K⁺ is 6.1 mEq/L. Best explanation?
qs.why: ACE inhibitor lowers aldosterone, spironolactone blocks its receptor, and CKD limits K⁺ excretion — risk compounds.
qs.discriminator: Check K⁺ and creatinine within 1 week of starting spironolactone.

qs.stem: A patient on lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) and hydrochlorothiazide starts daily naproxen for knee pain. Two weeks later, creatinine has risen sharply. What pattern explains this?

options.A: Expected COX-2 renal protection failing under stress
options.B: Bleeding from the NSAID plus the ACE inhibitor together
options.C: The “triple whammy”: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic causing AKI
options.D: A GI ulcer from NSAID plus diuretic, causing dehydration
options.E: Hepatotoxicity from NAPQI formed by naproxen metabolism

qs.why: NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise AKI risk, and adding a diuretic is the high-yield “triple whammy” AKI pattern (S36; S36 notes).

whys.A: COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney, and naproxen is nonselective (S28-29).
whys.B: NSAID + anticoagulant raises bleeding; this is a renal pattern (S36).
whys.C: NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise AKI risk, and adding a diuretic is the high-yield “triple whammy” AKI pattern (S36; S36 notes).
whys.D: NSAID + corticosteroid raises ulcer risk; this is a kidney injury pattern (S36).

qs.stem: A 70-year-old on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide, and lithium for bipolar disorder, starts daily naproxen for hip pain. Two weeks later he is confused and tremulous and his creatinine has risen. What best explains this?
qs.why: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is the ‘triple whammy’ for AKI, and NSAIDs raise lithium levels — the falling kidney function drives lithium toxicity (confusion, tremor).

whys.A: Doesn't explain the timing with naproxen.
whys.C: The pattern is renal, with lithium accumulation.

qs.takeaway: NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic → AKI; NSAIDs ↑ lithium.
qs.discriminator: One added drug, two interactions.
